title: Assignment and Increment
description: Shorthand for changing a variable, and the difference between count++ and ++count.

content.value: Changing a Variable by a Bit
In Module 2 you wrote `coins = coins + 5;`: read the value, add, store it back. Java has a shorthand for that: `coins += 5;` means exactly the same.

items.title: The long way
items.text: Read `coins`, add 5, store the answer back.

items.title: The shorthand
items.text: Does exactly the same work, with less typing.

content.title: Every operator has a shorthand
content.outro: Each one takes the variable, applies the operator with the value on the right, and stores the answer back.

content.value: The variable must already exist. `int score += 50;` is an error: a shorthand reads the old value first, and a brand new variable has none.

content.text: Each click adds exactly one. `count++` adds 1 and `count--` takes 1 away. You will see them in almost every loop from Module 5.

content.title: Three ways to add one, all identical. Use `++` for one, `+=` for anything else.

content.value: `++` can go before the name too: `++count`. On a line of its own, both are the same. The difference shows only when the value is used in the same instruction.

steps.note: `a++`: hand back the **old** value (5) to print, **then** add one.
`++b`: add one **first**, then hand back the new value (6).

content.title: Old value or new value?
content.outro: If the `++` comes after, the adding comes after. Both end at 6; only what was printed differs.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `x++` hands back the old value, 3, and only then adds one.

content.value: Keep increments on their own line. Two simple lines beat one clever line that needs a lesson to explain.
`+=` works on a `String` too, because `+` joins text. Each `+=` adds to the end.

content.caption: Fine for a handful of pieces. Thousands of `+=` in a loop is slow (each makes a new String); Module 7 shows the right tool.
Sample run: type `40` then `25` and it prints `Total so far: 65`. `total` starts at 0 so there is an old value to add to: every running total works this way.

practice.question: Start `int health = 100;` then take away 30 with `-=`, take away 25 more, and print the result after each change.
Predict what this prints before you run it, then run it and check.
Build the sentence `I am learning Java!` in a String using `+=` three times, then print it and its length.

quiz.question: What does `coins += 5;` mean?
options: Declare a new variable called coins holding 5.
quiz.explain: A shorthand reads the current value, applies the operator, and stores the answer back in the same variable.

quiz.question: `int score = 20;` then `score *= 3;`. What does score hold?
quiz.explain: `*=` multiplies the variable by the value on the right, so 20 becomes 60.

quiz.question: Which three lines all do the same thing?
quiz.explain: All three add one to the variable. `score++` is the usual way to write it when the amount is exactly one.

quiz.question: `int a = 5;` What does `System.out.println(a++);` print?
quiz.explain: With the `++` written after the name, the old value is handed back first and the increment happens after. `++a` would print 6.

quiz.question: Why does `int total += 5;` fail to compile?
options: A shorthand needs an existing value to read, and a new variable has none.
quiz.explain: `total += 5` means `total = total + 5`, which reads `total` before assigning to it. You cannot read a variable in the line that declares it.
